title: The afternoon slump
hookLine: the desert monks called it the noonday devil
tomorrow: what do you do at your own front door before walking in?

cards: The coffee's worn off. The email's been read and not answered. The window suddenly looks interesting, and so does the fridge, and so does anything happening in any other room.
A monk in the Egyptian desert, long ago, knew this hour so well that he gave it a name from a psalm: the noonday demon. Not because he thought tired people were possessed.
Because the pull felt like a voice, and a voice can be answered.

teach.b: The monk was Evagrius, and the thing he named was acedia. Listen to how physical he makes it. The sun seems to stand still.
The day feels endless. The monk keeps going to the window, watching for a visitor.
His small cell starts to look hateful, and so does his work, and so do the brothers he lives with, and a thought whispers that he'd be holier somewhere else.
In the Douay-Rheims, Psalm 90 promises protection from "the noonday devil." Bibles translated from the Hebrew read that line differently, but the desert monks prayed it this way.
The Catechism still names acedia among the temptations of prayer.
The desert's answer was plain: stay. Don't run from the cell; keep at the work.

teach.h: O GOD, COME TO MY ASSISTANCE.
teach.b: And John Cassian, who carried the desert teaching west, passed on one short psalm line for moments like this: "O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me."
Here's the thing to tell a friend: that same line still opens the hours of the Church's daily prayer, said by people in monasteries and parishes.
And Evagrius made a promise: whoever outlasts this demon comes through into a deep peace.

how: The Liturgy of the Hours opens each hour, including the midday prayer, with 'O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me,' and some Catholics use the line on its own when restlessness hits.

o: the nap monks took after their midday meal
the restless, heavy pull of mid-afternoon
the hottest hour, when fieldwork stopped

games.q: the desert hour — tap the pairs.
p: O God, come to my assistance

s: the desert monks thought sleepy people were possessed
they named a pull to quit what matters, so it could be resisted.
Cassian's line still opens the Church's daily hours
O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.
acedia whispers that you'd be holier somewhere else

games.q: your friend is three weeks into a new job. nothing's wrong, but every afternoon she's scrolling job listings. what would the desert say?
o: stay with it a while and see whether the pull passes.
leave soon; restlessness means it's the wrong place.
ignore the feeling and work twice as hard.
games.why: Evagrius said acedia whispers you'd be better somewhere else. the desert answer was to stay put and outlast it, with a short prayer.

practice: Stand and walk slowly for about a minute, feeling each foot land, the way a monk might pace a small cell without leaving it.
Going one way, say the first half of Cassian's line, O God, come to my assistance; coming back, the second, O Lord, make haste to help me. Then sit down where you started, and stay.
That staying is the whole desert teaching in one move.

wordCard.voice: The afternoon slump. The heavy, restless middle of the day, which the desert monks named acedia and learned to outlast.

orig.note: Greek: Evagrius's name for the restless midday pull, often rendered listlessness or sloth.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the noonday devil, easier to outlast once it has a name. See you tomorrow.
